content_of_post_to_comment: I've been following the Hank Green/ChatGPT debacle. If you didn't know, Hank Green is a science communicator on YouTube with a sizable following. On one of his videos, Green used some phrasing that sounded like ChatGPT-ese to some viewers. Apparently, "I appreciate the pushback" is an AI tell. Lots of viewers were calling him out for it. He decided to get ahead of the AI accusations and make a statement saying he ad-libbed the line and it was fully his. But then… he went on to say that he uses AI to help research topics, find papers and organize research. Not to write the scripts, just help with the boring bits. Then the feeding frenzy began. The anti-AI crowd treated his admission as a disclosure of fraud. The backlash is so severe, he's talking about pausing multiple channels while treating his AI use as if it were an addiction. Like using ChatGPT is the same as being addicted to heroin. He told his audience he needs to "come to terms with the fact that the level of dopamine I've been getting from interacting with LLMs is not healthy for me or good for the world." To be fair, a science communicator leaning on AI-generated notes does deserve some scrutiny. LLMs hallucinate sources and flatten nuance, and an educational channel should be careful to double check important information. The issue is what happened next. This situation is one of the clearest examples of what I call the honesty penalty. It's a warped incentive structure that punishes transparency and rewards concealment. Green was honest about what he did, acknowledged the criticism, and explained what he planned to change. He was rewarded with the worst backlash of his career. Every creator watching this right now is learning the same lesson: if you use AI, never disclose, lest they ruin your career too. If you get caught, deny it. If you can't deny it, treat it like a relapse. The one thing you absolutely cannot do is say you found AI useful or that you plan to keep using it in the future. That's socially impermissible right now. The penalty hurts the people who get caught. It also degrades the information environment for everyone else. If the only people talking publicly about AI use are the ones performing shame after getting exposed, the public never gets an accurate picture of how widespread and varied the actual use is. It's always a hidden sin. And the conversation stays stuck in moral panic mode instead of moving toward anything useful. The people who silently use AI and say nothing keep their reputations. The guy who told the truth is pausing his channels.
comment: The deeper issue may be that we lack a vocabulary for different kinds of AI use. Treating research assistance, drafting, and replacement as the same act makes honest disclosure almost impossible.
